summary:
Our project explores a local issue, drived mainly by salt exploitation, namely, residence disasters caused by landslides and ground movements.

Our idea came from a public distress article reported in romanian by the locals from Ocnele mari, an area near Râmnicu Vâlcea, Romania, describing a scene that impacted us emotionally and really looks like something horrific.. (ref: https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/social/ocnele-mari-noaptea-pocnesc-toate-alea-toate-incheieturile-la-casa-pocnesc-ma-sperie-179896).

Thus, we created an app meant to prevent issues of sorts through a demo being made for that local area specifically. We've taken data from NISAR, Sentinel-1 and a local station nearby found by exploring Muntean et. al 2026.

The application provides both a way to interpret prior information and a way of forecasting and prediction for disaster prevention using a time-series machine learning forecasting model (Chronos-2), it turns data into interpretable graphs, especially helping people that directly live nearby the exploatation areas (in the app's UI, areas linked from 1-4). In addition to that, it helps experienced persons further analyse and improve their understanding of the three sources of information, which complement each other and drive an expandable approach to further research, development & understanding of the local area presented.
details:
At the core of Dancing on Salt is Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), a remote-sensing technique that compares radar observations of the same location acquired at different times.

By analyzing differences in the radar signal, we can estimate very small surface displacements along the satellite's viewing direction.

Our platform combines two complementary missions:

  • NISAR (NASA–ISRO): A new L-band radar mission operating at a wavelength of approximately 24.4 cm. We processed 22 interferometric pairs covering observations between November 2025 and October 2026.
  • Sentinel-1 (ESA/Copernicus): An operational C-band radar mission operating at approximately 5.55 cm. Our processing pipeline incorporates observations from May 2025 through November 2026, with 374 interferometric processing jobs.

The measurements are processed using coherence filtering, atmospheric and elevation-related corrections, reference-area adjustments, and time-series reconstruction.

We also use European Ground Motion Service (EGMS) observations from 2020–2025 and ground-based GNSS measurements to establish historical context and independently evaluate our satellite-derived estimates.

The resulting measurements are converted into interactive geographical layers and time-series datasets, which power our publicly accessible web application.

What can users actually do?

Our application provides several interconnected features:

1. Interactive ground-deformation mapping

Users can explore Ocnele Mari through an interactive map displaying measured ground movement, satellite imagery, geographical boundaries, and four historically relevant investigation zones: Lacul Țeica, Țeica East, Ocnița–Goruniș, and Slătioarele.

Displacement is visualized using color-coded measurements, distinguishing movement toward and away from the observing satellite.

2. Satellite comparison

Users can switch between NISAR and Sentinel-1, examine morning and evening observation geometries, and compare measurements side by side over their shared observation window.

This makes it possible to investigate where different satellite observations support each other and where limitations prevent a reliable comparison.

3. Interactive historical timelines

Our acquisition timeline shows when each satellite observed the area, including periods with missing measurements. Users can animate ground movement through time rather than relying on a single static map.

4. Location-level and building-level exploration

Users can place a pin on the map, select an area, or interact with building outlines from OpenStreetMap to explore the available measurements around a location.

The application presents historical displacement, changes relative to nearby terrain, and plain-language interpretations. Where the signal is too uncertain, the interface identifies measurements below the noise threshold instead of claiming a confirmed movement.

5. AI-powered displacement forecasting

We integrated Chronos-2, a pretrained time-series forecasting model, to produce exploratory displacement projections based on the available historical measurements.

The platform displays measured versus predicted movement, forecast values, and evaluation information. These forecasts are explicitly presented as indicative estimates rather than reliable predictions of future hazards.

6. Scientific validation and transparency

Our application includes satellite coverage information, GNSS comparison stations, measurement-quality indicators, and documented validation checks.

Users can examine the evidence behind the visualizations, while technical reviewers can inspect our processing methodology, source data, and reproducible scripts.

We also developed a satellite-position visualization showing estimated satellite locations and upcoming observation passes over Ocnele Mari.

What did our analysis reveal?

One of our most important findings is the difference between historical evidence of subsidence and the ability of current satellite measurements to confirm it.

Historical EGMS measurements indicate approximately 18.9 mm/year of downward movement in the Ocnița–Goruniș investigation zone during 2020–2025.

However, our newer observations cannot yet establish an equally reliable ongoing trend in that zone.

NISAR's early measurements are affected by substantial noise, incomplete temporal coverage, and differences between observation geometries. Some Sentinel-1 measurements identify movement relative to surrounding terrain, but other zones lack sufficiently connected observations.

Rather than conceal these limitations, our application communicates them directly.

An important result of our project is not simply detecting movement, but identifying when the available evidence is insufficient to make a confident claim.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

Ground subsidence can damage homes, roads, utilities, and surrounding infrastructure. Yet the satellite measurements capable of studying these processes are often difficult for ordinary citizens to access and interpret.

Dancing on Salt aims to bridge that gap.

- For residents and prospective homeowners, the platform provides an accessible starting point for investigating historical ground movement near a location.

- For researchers and geospatial specialists, it offers a consolidated environment for comparing radar acquisitions, investigating deformation patterns, and examining measurement limitations.

- For local authorities and urban planners, it demonstrates how satellite observations could support preliminary geographical screening and help prioritize locations for further professional investigation.

Our longer-term vision is to extend the platform toward shareable location reports, broader geographical coverage, and monitoring notifications supported by sufficiently validated measurements.

The current application is an exploratory scientific tool, not an automated landslide-warning system, construction-safety assessment, or substitute for a geotechnical investigation.

What technologies did we use?

Our project combines satellite remote sensing, geodesy, machine learning, geospatial processing, and modern web development.

Satellite data and processing

  • NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GUNW radar interferograms.
  • ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar observations.
  • Alaska Satellite Facility's HyP3 InSAR processing service.
  • EGMS historical ground-motion products.
  • GNSS station observations and European velocity reference models.
  • Digital elevation and atmospheric information for measurement-quality investigations.

Scientific computing and machine learning

  • Python for radar processing, inversion, numerical analysis, and dataset generation.
  • NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, pyproj, and h5py for scientific and geospatial processing.
  • PyTorch and Amazon Chronos-2 for zero-shot time-series forecasting.
  • Statistical trend estimation, stable-ground comparisons, synthetic noise testing, and held-out forecast evaluation.

Application development

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • MapLibre GL JS for interactive geographical visualization.
  • OpenStreetMap, OpenFreeMap, and Esri World Imagery for geographical context.
  • GitHub for collaborative development and version control.
  • Vercel for public hosting.
  • Pytest and Playwright for automated validation and interface testing.

The forecasting pipeline can run on a CPU, while the satellite interferogram processing benefits from cloud-based services such as ASF HyP3.

What makes Dancing on Salt creative?

The originality of our approach lies in connecting satellite-derived measurements, scientific uncertainty, and everyday geographical questions in one accessible interface.

Traditional InSAR analysis requires specialized knowledge and software. We wanted to create a platform where someone could explore a geographical area and understand not only what was measured, but also how trustworthy that measurement is.

Our application combines two radar technologies with different wavelengths, observational histories, and acquisition geometries. It integrates historical and ground-based references, geographical exploration, and machine-learning forecasts.

Crucially, our design does not treat AI-generated forecasts as established facts. We expose measurement gaps, noisy observations, conflicting signals, and limitations in forecasting reliability.

The platform is therefore both a scientific visualization tool and a practical example of responsible interpretation of Earth observation data.

What factors did our team consider?

Our most important priority was scientific accuracy and responsible communication.

SAR measurements are influenced by atmospheric delays, terrain elevation, satellite viewing geometry, radar coherence, seasonal variation, and the stability of reference locations.

We investigated these factors through independent satellite comparisons, atmospheric-correction experiments, GNSS reference checks, synthetic noise experiments, and forecasting backtests.

We also considered data provenance, reproducibility, geographical accessibility, user experience, and the consequences of presenting uncertain scientific estimates to non-specialists.

Our ultimate vision is to help transform Earth observation data into practical geographical awareness: making the movement of the ground easier to see, easier to investigate, and easier to understand before consequential decisions are made.

Dancing on Salt begins with one small Romanian town, but the underlying problem can extend to communities around the world :)
